description: My name is Naheem Quadri. The purpose of this team is to develop a decision‑support tool that uses NASA Earth observations along with local soil information, crop characteristics, and farmer priorities to help farmers explore rotation strategies that could strengthen soil health and adapt their farms to changing conditions.
summary:
Ihayo is a free, phone-first website that helps Nigerian smallholder farmers compare crop rotation choices for the next seasons. The farmer picks a state and local government area and says what they grew in recent seasons, what matters most to them (for example less fertiliser, water saving or pests) and a few facts about the field.
Ihayo then reads 25 years of NASA POWER weather, NASADEM terrain, GPM IMERG satellite rain, SMAP soil moisture and MODIS and VIIRS vegetation records for that area. It combines them with modelled and laboratory soil data (iSDAsoil, ISRIC, iSDA samples), crop requirements and agronomy (FAO EcoCrop, FAO-56, IITA and ICRISAT guides) and real farm practice records (the Nigeria Agricultural Sample Survey 2023 and N2Africa trials). It returns up to three rotation choices, starting with the farmer's own rotation as the comparison. Each choice has a year-by-year plan, reasons, benefits, risks, what is not known and who to ask. Every statement links to a cited source with a confidence level. It answers the Field Shift challenge by combining NASA Earth observations with local soil information, crop characteristics and farmer priorities.
details:
What it does: The farmer answers one question per screen: place, past seasons (up to four, including fallow and intercrops), up to three priorities, and five short field questions (irrigation, Striga, waterlogging, labour, seed). Ihayo identifies the rotation the farmer follows and offers two additional alternatives. For each choice it shows a year-by-year plan, "may help" and "watch out" lines, how each choice meets the farmer's own priorities, how sure we are, and who to ask. A crop-fit score (0–100) shows how well each crop suits the land and weather. A weather what-if lets users change rain, rain start date and temperature and see how the growing season and crop fit move. It is clearly labelled as a re-run of the recorded weather, not a forecast. Users can see charts and a map, open the evidence behind each choice, and save a one-page text advice or a long report for the extension agent. The advice carries a fertiliser warning: do not buy fertiliser from this page.

How it works. An operator prepares data in advance for each local government area. The API itself downloads nothing while answering.


Climate: NASA POWER daily weather (2001–2025) gives usual rain, when the rains start and end, the length of the season in a usual and a shorter year, and the water balance (rain against crop water use by FAO-56). Years with implausible rain totals are flagged and left out.


Land: NASADEM gives elevation and slope. iSDAsoil gives modelled soil acidity, texture, carbon and fertility class with uncertainty ranges. Laboratory soil samples (ISRIC AfSP, iSDA) and a Nigerian digital soil map act as checks.


Crops: FAO EcoCrop ranges give the crop-fit score and reasons for each deduction. IITA and ICRISAT crop guides give Nigerian planting windows, fertiliser rates, pests and diseases. A trait table (364 rows) and a pest table (41 rows) each carry a source, a quote and a confidence level.


Rotations: a library of 26 options with 279 evidence rows, sequence rules, water measures and farmer cards. It is built from about 48 papers and reports (for example Franke 2018, Zhao 2022, Kureh 2006, Kamara 2019 and 2020, Uzoh 2019). Farm practice data from the Nigeria Agricultural Sample Survey 2023 and N2Africa trials show what farmers actually do.

Place: GRID3 geoBoundaries local government area outlines, with geopolitical zones, tie the advice to a place. Where an area has no prepared data, the farmer is offered the nearest area that has data, and every page says whose data it is. Confidence is graded H (Nigerian or West African primary source), M (global, review or older source), L (proxy) or G (a known gap).


Benefits. Farmers get a transparent comparison with their own rotation as the baseline, with reasons and limits written in plain words. Extension agents get a long report with evidence, a glossary and a review checklist. No account, name, phone number or exact location is asked.


Goal. To help farmers and agents have a better-informed conversation about the next season, and to make the uncertainty visible rather than hide it.


Tools. Python (uv), SQLAlchemy with SQLite (swappable through DATABASE_URL), Redis response cache , geopandas, xarray, earthaccess, a REST API with OpenAPI documentation, and a website hosted on Vercel.
